conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been vomiting nonstop since yesterday morning. I can’t keep anything down—water, food, nothing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any abdominal pain, fever, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no pain or fever. Just this awful nausea and vomiting. I had a really stressful day yesterday, and it started right after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of gastroparesis and Type 1 diabetes, this could be another flare-up. We’ll keep you NPO for now and give IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Last time, they thought it was gastroparesis too, but the tests were normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I saw your records. You had a normal gastric emptying study recently. But since you’re having the same symptoms, we’ll treat it supportively for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to eat soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’ll wait until your nausea improves. We’re giving you Zofran, Compazine, and Ativan through your IV to help control it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. My blood sugar’s probably high too—I couldn’t take my insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your glucose was 312 on arrival. We gave you some insulin and will adjust your regimen. The diabetes team will help fine-tune it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been worried about that. My sugars have been harder to control lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. Also, your blood pressure is quite high—172 over 112. That’s likely from the stress and not taking your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It always spikes in the hospital. I usually take lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving IV hydralazine to bring it down safely. Once you can take pills, we’ll restart your lisinopril and may add another medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling? Any nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, but maybe a little less. I haven’t vomited since last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep the anti-nausea meds going. Your labs show ketones in your urine, so your sugars are still a bit high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a sign your body’s using fat for energy because it can’t use glucose well. We’re adjusting your insulin to fix that. Your Lantus dose will go up from 28 to 31 units at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. Will I need to change my sliding scale too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the diabetes team is updating it to be more aggressive. We’ll give you the new instructions at discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to do a CT scan of your head. Since you can’t have an MRI because of your gastric pacer, this will help rule out any brain-related causes for the nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right—I forgot about that. The MRI was planned last time, but my doctor said the pacer makes it unsafe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The CT with contrast will be a good alternative. It’s quick and should give us the answers we need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the CT scan showed no masses, bleeding, or stroke. Just a small old lacune, unchanged from before. So nothing in your brain is causing the nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So it’s probably my gastroparesis again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely. Even though your last motility test was normal, symptoms can still flare. We’ll keep treating it as such.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try sipping water today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, let’s try small sips. If you keep it down for a few hours, we’ll advance to ice chips, then clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great—no vomiting, and you tolerated the clear liquids. We’re going to try a soft diet this evening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! I’m really hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just take it slow. We’ll still keep the anti-nausea meds on board for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning! You made it through the night without vomiting. Your blood sugar is also improving—staying in the 150s with the new insulin dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big improvement. What about my blood pressure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still a bit high, so we’ve added oral metoprolol twice daily. We’re also increasing your lisinopril to 20 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve never taken metoprolol before. Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can lower your heart rate and blood pressure. We’ll monitor it. Some people feel tired at first, but it usually settles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing so well—we’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What meds will I be going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your usual meds. Lantus is now 31 units at night. Lisinopril is 20 mg daily, and you’ll start metoprolol 50 mg twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have Zofran and Compazine tablets as needed. Plus, a new Compazine suppository—use it if pills don’t help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night went well—no nausea, good sleep. We’ll aim for discharge this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I see my endocrinologist soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, follow up with your PCP and endocrinologist within a week. They’ll review your insulin changes and monitor your blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set—you’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take the new meds as directed, advance your diet slowly, and call if nausea returns or your sugars go out of control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll schedule those follow-ups today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick final check before you leave. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really good. No nausea, ate breakfast without any issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’ve made excellent progress. Stay hydrated, keep monitoring your sugars, and don’t hesitate to reach out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up.
